strengths: Resolves a well-motivated open question (whether a finite, polynomial-in-d regret bound is achievable in online inverse linear optimization) for the broad and practically relevant class of M-convex action sets, improving the prior finite bound of exp(O(d log d)) to O(d log d).

The technical approach is elegant and clearly explained: it combines a clean structural characterization of optimality on M-convex sets (Proposition 2.4) with a volume-shrinking argument based on Grünbaum's theorem, and the warm-up O(d^2) algorithm nicely motivates the refined O(d log d) result before adding complexity.

The extension to adversarial corruption is a nice addition: the paper gives a corruption-robust bound of O((C+1) d log d) without requiring knowledge of C, using an elegant cycle-detection/restart mechanism on the induced directed graphs (Lemma 5.1, 5.2), with intuitive illustrative examples (Figure 2).

A matching (up to log d) Ω(d) lower bound is established for the M-convex setting, by embedding the general lower-bound construction of Sakaue et al. (2025b) into an M-convex instance via the M♮-convex to M-convex embedding, showing the upper bound is nearly tight.

The paper is well organized, proofs are rigorous and mostly self-contained, and the exposition carefully explains intuition (e.g., the mistake-bound argument, the role of M-convexity, and why curved action sets are trivial).
weaknesses: The contribution is restricted to M-convex action sets, a significant restriction relative to the general polyhedral/combinatorial feasible sets studied in prior work (Gollapudi et al. 2021; Sakaue et al. 2025b); the paper does not fully clarify how large a gap remains between M-convex and general settings, nor whether the techniques could partially extend beyond M-convexity.

No experimental or empirical validation is provided; all results are purely theoretical, and there is no illustration of how the O(d log d) bound behaves in practice or how tight the constants are, which limits practical assessment of significance.

The computational complexity of the algorithm is not fully practical: exact computation of the center of gravity is #P-hard, requiring an approximate randomized algorithm (Lovász and Vempala) whose own approximation-induced regret degradation is not rigorously analyzed in the main text (only briefly mentioned in a footnote), leaving a gap between the idealized regret bound and what an implementable algorithm would achieve.

The corruption model (simple count C of suboptimal rounds) is more restrictive than the cumulative suboptimality framework of Sakaue et al. (2025b); the authors acknowledge this is left as future work, but it somewhat limits the immediate applicability of the corruption-robust result.
The O(log d) gap between the O(d log d) upper bound and the Ω(d) lower bound is left open, and it's unclear from the current analysis whether this gap can be closed or is fundamental.

The novelty relative to prior work is somewhat incremental in places: the volume argument is explicitly borrowed from the contextual search/pricing literature (as the authors themselves note), and the restart-based corruption handling is conceptually similar to existing corruption-robust frameworks (e.g., Gupta et al. 2025), differing mainly in using M-convex structure for detection rather than maintaining parallel copies.

strengths: The paper makes genuine technical progress on a well-motivated open problem: whether a finite regret bound polynomial in d (rather than exponential, as in Gollapudi et al. 2021, or log T-dependent, as in prior work) is achievable in online inverse linear optimization. Restricting to M-convex action sets, the authors give a positive answer with an O(d log d) bound.

The technical approach is elegant: it combines a clean structural fact about M-convex sets (Proposition 2.4, the local-exchange optimality characterization) with a volume-shrinking argument based on Grünbaum's theorem, in a way that is specific and non-trivial (the mistake bound O(d^2) from a naive pairwise-ordering argument is improved to O(d log d) via order-simplex volume bounds).

The corruption-robust extension (Section 5) is a nice complement: using acyclicity of a directed graph built from feedback to detect corruption and trigger restarts, achieving O((C+1)d log d) without needing to know C in advance. The two supporting lemmas (5.1, 5.2) are proven carefully and the mechanism is intuitive (illustrated well by Figure 2).

A matching lower bound of Ω(d) is established for the M-convex setting by adapting a prior construction (Sakaue et al. 2025b) via an M♮-convex-to-M-convex embedding trick, showing the upper bound is tight up to a log d factor.

The paper is well organized, with a warm-up O(d^2) algorithm before the refined O(d log d) result, aiding readability, and a reasonably thorough related-work/comparison table (Table 1) situating the contribution against prior regret bounds.
weaknesses: The paper is purely theoretical with no experiments or numerical illustration whatsoever, not even a toy simulation to sanity-check the constants in the O(d log d) bound or to compare practically against the exp(d log d) bound of Gollapudi et al. or the O(d log T) bound of Sakaue et al. This makes it hard to gauge whether the improvement is meaningful for realistic T, d.

The central algorithm (Algorithm 1/2) requires computing (an approximation of) the center of gravity of a polytope Pt at every round, which is #P-hard to compute exactly (as the paper itself notes) and requires randomized approximate algorithms (Lovász–Vempala). The paper only gestures at this via a footnote (footnote 4) and a brief paragraph on time complexity; a full, explicit theorem quantifying how approximate-center-of-gravity errors compound into the final regret bound is not given, leaving the practical/algorithmic guarantee somewhat informal.

The scope of the main positive result is restricted to M-convex action sets, a fairly special (albeit broad) subclass of the general polytopes/action sets considered in prior work (Bärmann et al., Besbes et al., Sakaue et al. 2025b). The paper explicitly frames this as only a 'partial' resolution of the open problem, and it remains unclear whether the M-convexity assumption is doing genuinely fundamental work here or is simply the largest class for which existing volume-argument machinery happens to apply cleanly; the paper does not explore whether weaker structural assumptions could suffice.

There is a residual O(log d) gap between the upper (O(d log d)) and lower (Ω(d)) bounds that is left open, so the 'tightness' claim in the abstract/intro is only up to this factor; combined with the restriction to M-convex sets, the overall resolution of the stated open question is incremental rather than complete.

The corruption-robust algorithm restarts by discarding the entire arc set At upon detecting a cycle, which is a relatively blunt way to handle corruption and likely wastes previously accumulated correct information; the paper does not compare against or discuss whether a less wasteful correction mechanism (e.g., localized repair of At rather than full restart) could yield a better dependence on C.

The technical novelty is primarily a combination of existing tools (Grünbaum's theorem/volume arguments from the contextual search literature, and known M-convex structural results from discrete convex analysis) rather than a fundamentally new technique; the authors are transparent about this borrowing, but it somewhat limits the paper's originality contribution beyond the specific synthesis achieved.

strengths: The paper makes clear technical progress on a well-motivated open question (existence of a regret bound for online inverse linear optimization that is both finite and polynomial in the dimension d), providing a novel O(d log d) upper bound under the M-convex action set restriction, essentially closing the gap up to a log d factor via a matching Ω(d) lower bound (Theorem 6.1).

The core technical idea—combining the structural optimality characterization for M-convex sets (Proposition 2.4) with a volume-shrinking argument based on Grünbaum's theorem—is elegant and clearly explained. The paper nicely builds intuition first via a simple O(d^2) algorithm (Section 3) before refining to O(d log d) (Section 4), which aids readability and helps referees/readers verify correctness.

The extension to adversarially corrupted feedback (Section 5) is a nontrivial and practically relevant addition. The mechanism of monitoring acyclicity of an induced directed graph to detect corruption and trigger restarts, without requiring prior knowledge of C, is a clean and well-justified idea (Lemmas 5.1 and 5.2), and the resulting O((C+1)d log d) bound smoothly recovers the uncorrupted case.

The paper is well situated in the literature: Table 1 crisply summarizes prior regret bounds, and connections to the contextual search/pricing literature (borrowing the volume argument) and discrete convex analysis (M-convexity) are clearly drawn, along with concrete examples (matroids, integer-lattice extensions) that ground the abstract M-convexity assumption in familiar combinatorial structures.

Proofs appear complete and are given in full within the main text rather than deferred, and time-complexity considerations (including the #P-hardness caveat for exact center-of-gravity computation and the use of approximate polynomial-time sampling algorithms) are honestly discussed.
weaknesses: The contribution is restricted entirely to M-convex action sets. Although the authors motivate this class (matroids, integer-lattice extensions) and explicitly call the result a 'partial' resolution of the open problem, it remains unclear how large a fraction of practically relevant instances (e.g., general polytopes, knapsack-type constraints, and other non-M-convex combinatorial sets used in contextual recommendation applications) fall outside this class, somewhat limiting the immediate applicability of the results.

No empirical evaluation or simulation is provided to illustrate the practical behavior of the proposed algorithms (e.g., how tight the O(d log d) bound is in practice, or how the corruption-detection/restart mechanism behaves under different corruption patterns). Given that the paper explicitly targets a 'practically meaningful' regret bound (as emphasized in the introduction), some experimental validation, even on small synthetic matroid instances, would strengthen the practical claims.

The exact algorithm relies on computing (or approximating) the center of gravity of a polytope at every round, which is #P-hard in general; the authors note that approximate randomized sampling algorithms (Lovász–Vempala) can be used instead, but do not analyze how the approximation error in this step propagates into the stated regret bound, leaving a gap between the idealized regret bound and what is achievable by a fully specified, efficient implementation.

The novelty of individual technical ingredients (Grünbaum's theorem based volume argument, borrowed from the contextual search/pricing literature; Murota's structural characterization of M-convex optimality) is somewhat incremental, as acknowledged by the authors themselves; the primary contribution is the synthesis of these known tools rather than a fundamentally new proof technique.

An O(log d) gap remains between the achieved upper bound and the proven lower bound, and the corruption-robust bound's linear dependence on C (rather than possibly sublinear or with more refined dependence on corruption magnitude) is not shown to be tight, leaving open whether the current bounds represent the true optimal rates in this class.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated open question in online inverse linear optimization: whether a finite regret bound polynomial in dimension d is achievable, providing a positive partial answer for the broad class of M-convex action sets (which includes matroids and various combinatorial structures).

The technical approach is elegant: combining a known structural characterization of M-convex optimality (Proposition 2.4) with a volume-shrinking argument based on Grünbaum's theorem yields a clean progression from an O(d^2) warm-up algorithm to the sharper O(d log d) bound.

The corruption-robust extension is a nice contribution: by monitoring acyclicity of a directed graph built from feedback, the algorithm detects corruption and restarts without needing prior knowledge of the corruption budget C, achieving O((C+1) d log d) regret.

A matching Ω(d) lower bound (adapted from prior work via an M-convex embedding of the hard instance) shows the upper bound is tight up to a log d factor, giving a fairly complete picture for this action-set class.

The paper is generally well organized, with clear illustrative examples (matroids, extensions to integer lattices), a helpful comparison table against prior regret bounds, and a fairly complete treatment of computational costs, tie-breaking, and even a small numerical experiment to substantiate practical relevance.
weaknesses: The contribution only partially resolves the stated open problem: results are restricted to the special (though broad) class of M-convex action sets, not the general polyhedral/combinatorial feasible sets considered in prior work (Gollapudi et al., Sakaue et al.), so the core open question for general action sets remains unresolved.

The main technical tool (the volume/Grünbaum argument) is explicitly borrowed from the contextual search/pricing literature (Gollapudi et al. 2021; Paes Leme and Schneider 2022); the paper's novelty is mainly in combining this with the known M-convex exchange characterization, which, while useful, is a comparatively incremental synthesis rather than a fundamentally new technique.

Computing the exact center of gravity used for the sharper O(d log d) bound is #P-hard, and the polynomial-time approximate implementation described in the appendix has very high overhead (roughly O(d^6 log d · log T) per round), raising concerns about the practical usability of the refined algorithm despite its favorable asymptotic regret.
The Ω(log d) gap between the O(d log d) upper bound and the Ω(d) lower bound is left open, and it is unclear whether this gap can be closed, tempering the tightness claim.

Empirical validation is very limited: a single small synthetic experiment with time-varying uniform matroids (d=20) is reported, which is insufficient to assess robustness of the theoretical gains across richer M-convex structures (e.g., graphic matroids, integer-lattice extensions) or to validate the corruption-robust algorithm's practical performance under adversarial corruption.

The treatment of tied components in w*, while carefully discussed in the appendix, reveals that the corruption-detection mechanism fundamentally relies on strict distinctness of objective components, which may be a nontrivial assumption in practice and is not required in competing approaches (e.g., Sakaue et al. 2025b's O(d log T) bound handles corruption without such an assumption).
